hook_text: The shop owner works there every day. So why is her pay never recorded as wages?
clip_script: Every rand a shop pays out goes into one notebook: the cash payments journal. Each line: the proof, the day, who was paid, the amount in the bank column. Then the payment needs a home. Two questions find it. Will a customer buy this? Then it is trading stock. Is it pay for an employee? Then it is wages. Everything else goes in sundry with its name. New shelves for the shop? Customers do not buy the shelves, so it is equipment. And the owner sending R2 000 to her own account? She works there every day, but she is not an employee. You cannot employ yourself. So it is drawings. At the end of March, Ridgeview Hardware paid out R56 590 and received R140 250. Money in minus money out: R83 660 left in the bank. Two notebooks, one bank balance, and the numbers agree.
visual_style: Payments drop like parcels onto a sorting table with three bins labelled trading stock, wages and sundry; a shelf unit bounces off the stock bin into equipment; a final subtraction on a whiteboard.
mood: Brisk, clear, a little playful at the sorting.
pacing: Fast sorting rhythm, a beat on the owner question, a satisfying final subtraction.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort a month of payments yourself.
